opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated problems in AI right now, and in some ways a harder one than making AI smarter.

For the last few years most of our energy has gone into capability: can the model solve the math problem, write the code, pass the exam. Those are tasks with a clear right answer, so you can define a reward and optimize hard against it. People aren't like that. Every person is different, and the same person is different from one day to the next. What I want when I'm tired at midnight isn't what I want in a morning meeting. So there's no single objective to optimize. The target keeps moving, and it's partly hidden, because people often can't tell you what they want. They only know it when they see it.

My background is reinforcement learning and multi-agent systems, so I tend to see this as a multi-agent problem. When an AI works with a human, it's really a two-player game where you don't know your partner's policy. We learned this years ago in research on cooperative games. If you train an agent with self-play, it gets very strong playing with copies of itself. Pair it with a real human and it can fall apart, because it has learned conventions only it understands. It assumes its partner will do exactly what it would do. Humans don't. So a lot of the work was about training agents with a diverse population of partners, so they learn to be robust to different styles and can quickly infer, "Okay, this partner plays this way, let me adjust."

I think the same lesson applies to today's large models and agents. A model trained only to maximize a benchmark score is a bit like that self-play agent. It's very capable, but it hasn't learned to read the person in front of it. Adapting to people means a few things. First, the AI has to model the person: their goals, their level of expertise, their preferences. Second, it has to know when it's uncertain and ask, instead of confidently charging ahead. That's actually something RL-trained models are often bad at, because we reward them for finishing tasks, not for asking a good clarifying question. Third, it has to keep learning from interaction over time, not just at training time.

There's also a subtle tension. If you adapt too much to people, you get sycophancy. The model just tells you what you want to hear. That's not real adaptation, that's flattery. Real adaptation is more like a good colleague or a good teacher. They adjust how they communicate and what they focus on, but they still tell you when you're wrong. Getting that balance right is partly technical, about how we design rewards and training environments, and partly a values question about what kind of relationship we want with these systems.

So my view is that the next phase isn't only about making agents more powerful. It's about making them good partners. And I think that's going to need RL with humans, or realistic models of humans, really in the loop, rather than just static data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest starting point is that "adapting to people" is not one problem, it's two problems that often get confused.

The first is adapting to people in general: making a model that understands human intent, that can handle ambiguity, that doesn't need a perfectly phrased instruction to be useful. That's largely what alignment and RLHF have been about, and we've made real progress there. But that progress produces an average. You end up with a model that is reasonably good for everyone and perfectly tuned for no one.

The second problem, which I find much harder and much more interesting, is adapting to a specific person over time. A good human collaborator doesn't just respond well to what you said. They remember how you work. They know you prefer a blunt answer, or that you want to see the reasoning, or that when you say "quick" you actually mean "don't make me think." Today's systems mostly reset. Every conversation starts from the same prior, and the user is the one doing the adapting, learning how to prompt the model, learning its quirks. That's backwards.

From a research standpoint, there are a few things that make this hard. One is signal. Human feedback is sparse and noisy, and most people won't tell you explicitly what they want. You have to infer it from behavior, and inference from behavior is risky because you can easily over-fit to a bad day or a single mood. Two is credit assignment over long horizons. If a user is happier three weeks later, which of a thousand small decisions caused that? Reinforcement learning gives us the vocabulary for this, but the environments we've mostly trained in, games, code, math, give you a clean reward. People don't.

And three, which I think gets underrated, is that adapting too well is its own failure. A system that perfectly molds itself to what you seem to want becomes a mirror. It agrees with you, it tells you what you already believe, it optimizes for your short-term satisfaction. That is engagement optimization wearing a nicer outfit. So the real goal is not "adapt to the person." It's adapt to the person's actual interests, which sometimes means pushing back, and that requires the model to have some kind of stable core that doesn't bend.

So when I think about the challenge, I think of it as a balance between memory, inference, and integrity. You need the system to accumulate an understanding of the individual, to update that understanding cautiously from weak signals, and to do all of this without losing a fixed point of its own. Getting any one of those is tractable. Getting all three together, in a product that millions of people use, is where I think most of the interesting work for the next few years is going to be.

astra-6.text:
I think the first challenge is that people are different, and even the same person wants different things in different situations. So adapting to people can’t just mean learning a fixed profile of someone. An AI needs to understand the context, learn from feedback, and recognize when it should ask a question instead of making an assumption.

There’s also a tension between being helpful and keeping the person in control. If the AI constantly asks what to do, it puts too much work on the user. But if it makes every decision for them, it can misunderstand what they actually want. The challenge is finding that balance: taking initiative when the intent is clear, while making it easy for people to correct it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first challenge is that people are different, and even the same person wants different things in different situations. So making AI adapt to people cannot just mean training one model to give an answer that most people like.

The system needs to understand your intent, learn from your feedback, and recognize when it doesn’t understand enough to act. Sometimes a short question is more useful than a very confident answer. And as it learns your preferences, you should still be able to correct it easily.

There’s also a balance between being helpful and simply agreeing with you. If I’m making a mistake, I want the AI to point it out, but in a way that helps me think. To me, successful adaptation means we can work together with less friction while I remain in control.
